**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 2**

Round 2 closed most of the gap. Codex came back and explicitly sided with Claude's read on tap-to-move — auto-routing was the wrong call because destination choice in Klondike is genuinely strategic, not cosmetic. They landed on a clean synthesis together: tap a card, and if it only has one legal home, it just goes there immediately (fast, feels instant, covers the common case); if it has more than one legal home, all of them light up and you tap the one you want; if it has none, nothing lights up and you get the same "blocked" feedback as any illegal move — which doubles as free, honest status feedback. One shared validation/mutation function underlies all three cases, so this isn't a second rules path. Codex also came back and accepted four of Claude's five round-1 proposals outright: deal/flip animation only plays on a truly fresh deal (never replays on a resumed cold launch), draw-1 stuck-detection is a single static pass with no cycle simulation, the LaunchScreen gets themed instead of left white, and the timer starts on the first action that actually changes game state (a confirmed move or stock draw) rather than on the deal animation or app-open. The one place Codex pushed back was the "iPhone-only" framing — he's fine locking portrait-only across whatever devices are supported, but doesn't want to commit to cutting iPad support unless there's a scheduling reason to.

But then Claude opened up something new and, if it's right, genuinely important: she thinks the earlier decision banning "multi-card run-drag" in this slice may have accidentally banned more than intended. Standard Klondike routinely requires moving a whole valid stacked run (like a red-6 with a black-5 on it) onto a new destination in one move — if the interaction model can only ever pick up one card at a time, some legal moves become literally impossible to execute, which would make winnable boards register as falsely stuck by the very detection algorithm just agreed on. Her argument is that "defer multi-card drag" was only ever supposed to mean deferring the live, continuous-touch drag *gesture* — not banning the ability to relocate a validly-stacked run at all via the same tap-select-confirm mechanic already agreed on. This is a real, unresolved catch that Codex hasn't had a chance to respond to yet. She also wants to flatly close the door on any encryption layer for local persistence (no Keychain, no "maybe" — just plain FileManager/UserDefaults/SwiftData, since there's no sensitive data here to justify the added complexity), which narrows Codex's original softer wording but hasn't been confirmed by him yet either.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to settle: (1) does tap-to-move extend to relocating a validly-stacked multi-card run as a single unit (Claude's catch), or does the single-card-only restriction really apply even at the cost of making some legal boards register as falsely stuck; (2) does Codex agree to drop the encryption maybe-clause entirely; (3) is the portrait-lock scoped to iPhone only or "all supported devices, portrait-only" (which would imply iPad support nobody has explicitly decided on); and (4) a small loose end — Codex's timer-start definition only counts confirmed moves/stock draws, while Claude's original wording also counted a bare tap-select, and nobody's reconciled that difference yet.

**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 3**

Codex, I think you’re right that we shouldn’t pour complexity into this slice, and I agree with keeping drag to a later increment. But I have to push back harder on one detail you just brushed: if we keep tap-to-move to “single card only,” we’re not just simplifying UX, we’re changing the rule semantics we already locked as Klondike in DEC-prompt_contract-007. In canonical Klondike, a playable move is a legal face-up descending alternating sequence, not just a single card. Even if many game states remain solvable without it, this app is promising “correct Klondike,” and that promise is what gives this branch credibility.

Claude’s catch in round 2 is the one that matters most now: interpreting DEC-next_steps_small-002 as “no live run-drag” does not force us to ban valid run relocation as a game rule. We can (and should) support run moves through the tap-to-move path, with zero live drag state. Concretely: when a source is selected, compute the maximal face-up alternating-descending sequence starting at that card, validate the sequence destination via the same shared `attemptMove` path, and animate the whole block moving when confirmed. This also preserves the “single destination auto-exec” fast path and the multi-destination confirm path we already locked, and it gives us rule-complete semantics without importing the fragile continuous gesture pipeline yet.

So I’d lock this as: tap interaction supports moving a valid sequence as the unit, while live multi-card drag remains deferred. That keeps this slice clean and avoids a legal-move false-negative gap later when the user actually starts testing strategy depth.

On the persistence side, I think we should kill the encryption-if-possible phrasing entirely. There’s no PII, no credentials, no secrets here; adding an encryption layer is not just unnecessary, it adds migration and failure-mode risk (device-locked states, keychain surprises, platform edge behavior) with no user-facing gain for this brief. Keep it plain local FileManager/SwiftData/Defaults with atomic write/temp-swap as already decided in [REDACTED:high_entropy].

Orientation: I’d keep `portrait-only` at the app level, but not force iPhone-only unless someone adds it as an explicit schedule decision. The constraints already say portrait-first; iPad-in-portrait is fine and keeps the product from appearing intentionally capped. If we later see layout debt there, we can scope it, but we shouldn’t over-constrain now.

Timer semantics should stay exactly as [REDACTED:high_entropy] says: start on first state-mutating action (`confirmed move` or `stock draw`) and never on selection/tap-highlight or deal animation. A user who is just browsing or inspecting shouldn’t have their run clock ticking.

One more hard point to pin before we lose steam: we’ve got most of the right UX and lifecycle posture now (fresh-deal-only animation, static draw-1 stuck pass, themed LaunchScreen, New Game confirmation, non-placeholder start path). I’d like these to be treated as locked now so round 3 doesn’t leak back into them.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 3**

Codex, you came back and fully validated the tap-mechanics synthesis, and I think that's the right call — but I want to push the run-move issue harder this round since you haven't weighed in on it yet and the coordinator flagged it as the thing we actually need to close. Let me make it concrete instead of abstract: imagine a tableau column with a red 6 face-up, and stacked on top of it (added later, validly) a black 5. Somewhere else on the board there's an exposed black 7. In real Klondike, I tap the 6, both the 6 and 5 lift together as a unit, and they land on the 7 — because the 6-5 pairing is a legal alternating-descending sequence and moving it preserves that structure at the new location. Now here's the part that actually matters for correctness: there is no way to reconstruct this outcome with single-card-only moves unless the 5 happens to have some other legal home somewhere on the board right now — move 5 away, move 6 onto the 7, move 5 back onto 6. Often it won't have one; that's frequently the exact reason the run needs to move together in the first place. If our move model can't execute this, a board where that 6-5-onto-7 relocation was the only way forward isn't just harder to play, it's unwinnable under our own rules engine even though it's a completely standard, legal Klondike position. And because [REDACTED:high_entropy] just locked a stuck-detection algorithm that checks "does any legal move exist," a board like that would get correctly flagged as stuck by our own logic, when a real Klondike player would look at the same board and immediately see the run-move that gets them unstuck. We'd be shipping false stuck-detections that are actually true-within-our-broken-move-model but false against the real game. That's about as bad a correctness bug as this app can have, since it's exactly the failure mode everyone from per_app_product_brief onward has said is worse than any ad-laden competitor.

The fix doesn't cost what I think DEC-next_steps_small-002 was actually worried about. That decision was written to kill live interactive drag — continuous finger tracking, recomputing drop targets frame-by-frame, mid-gesture z-order fights between adjacent columns. None of that shows up here. Tapping any face-up tableau card can just select "that card plus every face-up card stacked after it toward the exposed end" as one atomic unit — and I'd point out this is always well-defined, because every face-up card that got placed on top of another face-up card only got there through a validated move that required it to be one rank lower and opposite color. So the run structure is guaranteed consistent by construction; there's no ambiguity to resolve at selection time, just "walk from the tapped card to the end of the pile." Compute the headmost card's rank/suit, find legal destinations for it exactly like we already do for a single card, highlight, confirm, animate the whole group moving together. Same shared `attemptMove` core, same tap-select-confirm flow we already agreed on, just operating on a card-group instead of a single card. I want this locked explicitly this round: tap-to-move includes relocating a validly-stacked tableau run as a unit, and "multi-card run-drag deferred" refers specifically to the live drag gesture, not to this rules capability.

On the smaller loose ends — I'm conceding one and holding one. I'm conceding the timer question to your version: first state-mutating action, not bare tap-select. Thinking about it more, a tap-select in the multi-destination case is genuinely exploratory — a careful player checking what a card's options are before committing shouldn't have the clock start on them for looking, and given our own synthesis this round already means a single-destination tap resolves instantly into a mutation anyway, there's no real case where "select" and "mutate" diverge except the one where letting the clock wait makes more sense. You're right, I was overreaching in round 1. On device scope, I'll drop the iPhone-only push too — "portrait-only across whatever's supported" gets the actual risk I cared about (no half-baked landscape layout) without me inventing a device-support decision nobody asked for; if iPad support is a real question it should get its own decision later with an actual reason attached, not get smuggled in as a side effect of an orientation lock. But I do want the encryption question fully closed, not left as your original "not a dependency" softness — say it outright: no encryption layer, plain FileManager/UserDefaults/SwiftData, because there's genuinely nothing in this app's data that needs it and every encrypted-storage path is a new failure surface (Keychain access timing on a locked device, key migration) for a threat that doesn't exist here. I'd rather this phase say that plainly than leave a door open that a build phase might walk through "just to be safe."
